claim: The 23 bp TerB sequence in interaction with the Tus protein have been successfully used in yeast and mice to create artificial RFBs.
source: The 23 bp TerB sequence in interaction with the Tus protein have been successfully used in yeast and mice to create artificial RFBs (Larsen et al., 2014a; Willis et al., 2018; Willis et al., 2017; Willis et al., 2014; Willis and Scully, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work in yeast and mice.

claim: MCF7 5C-TerB clone has a unique integrated copy of the pWB15 plasmid carrying two sets of five TerB repeat sequences in opposite, non-permissive orientations.
source: To study the effect of site-specific replication blocks at a genomic locus in human cells, we used a previously established MCF7 clone with a unique integrated copy of the pWB15 plasmid carrying two sets of five TerB repeat sequences in opposite, non-permissive orientations with respect to the incoming replication forks (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to the experimental system described and shown in figures.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing confirmed the single-copy integration of the plasmid at hg38 chr12:95325001.
source: Whole-genome sequencing of the clone was carried out to confirm the single-copy integration of the plasmid at hg38 chr12:95325001.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data.

claim: Tus signal is specifically enriched over 20 times compared to the vector control condition in proximity to the TerB sequences.
source: The Tus signal is specifically enriched over 20 times compared to the vector control (VC) condition in proximity to the TerB sequences (PP9, 2, and 47) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 19% of the cells transfected with the two tagged Tus were harboring one or two PLA signal versus 9% of the cells transfected with the VC.
source: We observed 19% of the cells transfected with the two tagged Tus were harboring one or two PLA signal versus 9% of the cells transfected with the VC (Figure 1E), a significant enrichment of the PLA signal when Tus was bound to TerB.
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The binding of Tus protein with the TerB sequences indicates a specific interaction in human cells.
source: These results indicate a specific interaction of the Tus protein with the TerB sequences in human cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ChIP and PLA data presented.

claim: The Tus-TerB interaction can induce an RFB in mouse embryonic cells using a chromosomally integrated system.
source: It has previously been demonstrated that the Tus-TerB interaction can induce an RFB in mouse embryonic cells using a chromosomally integrated system (Willis et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: When Tus was expressed, transition sites were found accumulated near the TerB regions compared to the random signal spread on the 200 kb region when Tus is not expressed.
source: When Tus was expressed, these transition sites were found accumulated near the TerB regions (Figure 2D, arrows within the white oval) compared to the random signal spread on the 200 kb region when Tus is not expressed (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SMARD data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: The binding of Tus on TerB arrays can impair the replisome progression at genomic loci.
source: We quantified the percentage of molecules with replication forks at each 5 kb interval in the 200 kb SfiI segment containing TerB sequences (Figure 2E and F) and confirmed an accumulation of forks at the TerB sequences only when Tus was expressed (Figure 2F, black arrow), supporting that the binding of Tus on TerB arrays can impair the replisome progression at genomic loci.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of SMARD data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: Expression of the Tus protein alone does not alter the direction of replication fork progression along the 200 kb SfiI segment.
source: Interestingly, expression of the Tus protein alone does not alter the direction of replication fork progression along the 200 kb SfiI segment where forks predominantly progress from the 3′ to 5′ direction in cells both with and without Tus expression as analyzed by the percentage of molecules with IdU incorporation at each 5 kb interval (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by replication profile data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: No significant difference was observed in the global replication fork speed in cells with or without Tus expression.
source: Furthermore, no significant difference was observed in the global replication fork speed in cells with or without Tus expression (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: When Tus bound the TerB sequences integrated within chromosome 12, it creates a physical barrier and an obstacle to the replication fork progression.
source: Together, these data indicate that when Tus bound the TerB sequences integrated within chromosome 12, it creates a physical barrier and an obstacle to the replication fork progression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the SMARD and ChIP data presented.

claim: MCM3 was threefold more enriched upstream of the TerB arrays at the PP0-2 and PP10 sites compared to the surrounding primer pairs when Tus was expressed.
source: When Tus was expressed, MCM3 was threefold more enriched upstream of the TerB arrays at the PP0-2 and PP10 sites compared to the surrounding primer pairs (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: There is an enrichment of the DNA repair scaffold protein FANCM at the TerB sites mirroring the MCM3 enrichment.
source: Additionally, we find that there is an enrichment of the DNA repair scaffold protein FANCM at the TerB sites mirroring the MCM3 enrichment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicative of the stalled replication forks as previously described (Collis et al., 2008; Nandi and Whitby, 2012; Panday et al., 2021; Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citations to prior work.

claim: Tus expression induces an RFB at the TerB arrays impairing the replisome progression during S-phase.
source: Together, these results show that Tus expression induces an RFB at the TerB arrays impairing the replisome progression during S-phase.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the MCM3 and FANCM enrichment data.

claim: One of the earliest responses to replication stress is the phosphorylation of the histone variant H2AX on serine 139 (γH2AX) by members of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)-like family (PIKK).
source: One of the earliest responses to replication stress is the phosphorylation of the histone variant H2AX on serine 139 (γH2AX) by members of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)-like family (PIKK) (Ward and Chen, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: GFP-Tus and γH2AX were immunoprecipitated together using GFP or γH2AX antibodies.
source: Using a co-immunoprecipitation assay with the chromatin fraction of cross-linked cells expressing either GFP tag or GFP-Tus, we found that GFP-Tus and γH2AX were immunoprecipitated together using GFP or γH2AX antibodies (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 16% of the HA-Tus transfected cells were harboring at least one PLA signal versus 3% of the VC transfected cells.
source: We found that 16% of the HA-Tus transfected cells were harboring at least one PLA signal versus 3% of the VC transfected cells (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: γH2AX is enriched strictly co-localizing with the Tus-Ter interaction sites (PP9 and PP47), suggesting a local role of γH2AX in response to stalled RFs.
source: We observed an enrichment of γH2AX, strictly co-localizing with the Tus-Ter interaction sites (PP9 and PP47), suggesting a local role of γH2AX in response to stalled RFs (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The γH2AX signal after a site-directed DSB spreads, in contrast to the very tight local signal observed at the Tus-TerB RFB.
source: This is in stark contrast to the observed spreading of the γH2AX signal after a site-directed DSB (Berkovich et al., 2007; Chailleux et al., 2014; Clouaire et al., 2018; Savic et al., 2009). To corroborate this observation in our integrated cassette, we generated a site-specific DSB by expressing Cas9 targeted to the integrated cassette (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C). We assessed γH2AX using the ChIP-qPCR assay 24 hr after transfection and noticed enrichment at the distal primer pairs (PP0-2 and PP10), contrasting with the very tight local signal observed at the Tus-TerB RFB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ChIP-qPCR data for Cas9-induced DSB versus Tus-TerB RFB, and citations to prior work.

claim: No significant γH2AX signal was found between VC or Tus expression, supporting the lack of global response.
source: However, we did not find any significant γH2AX signal between VC or Tus expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B), supporting the lack of global response.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The RFB generated by the interaction between Tus and the TerB arrays activates a stress response that stimulates the phosphorylation of H2AX, concentrated around the fork block.
source: This suggests that the RFB generated by the interaction between Tus and the TerB arrays activates a stress response that stimulates the phosphorylation of H2AX, concentrated around the fork block.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the γH2AX enrichment data at TerB sites.

claim: ATR is known to phosphorylate H2AX in response to replication stress and plays a pivotal role in the surveillance of DNA replication.
source: ATR is known to phosphorylate H2AX in response to replication stress and plays a pivotal role in the surveillance of DNA replication (Ward and Chen, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Tus expression alone did not activate the global ATR-dependent checkpoint as the level of phospho-protein remained the same as the VC control.
source: Tus expression alone did not activate the global ATR-dependent checkpoint as the level of phospho-protein remained the same as the VC control (Figure 4A, lanes 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No observable difference in cell cycle progression was found between VC or Tus expression alone, supporting the lack of global response.
source: We did not find any observable difference in cell cycle progression between VC or Tus expression alone (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B), supporting the lack of global response.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A 4 hr treatment with ATRi reduced the level of phospho-ATR TH1989, reflecting a decrease in ATR activity.
source: A 4 hr treatment with ATRi reduced the level of phospho-ATR TH1989, reflecting a decrease in ATR activity (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The γH2AX enrichment in the vicinity of TerB sites after Tus expression was remarkably decreased upon ATRi treatment.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the γH2AX enrichment in the vicinity of TerB sites after Tus expression was remarkably decreased upon ATRi treatment (Figure 4C–E, PP9 and PP47), implying that the Tus-TerB RFB activates a localized stress response that stimulated the local phosphorylation of H2AX.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: The Tus-TerB RFB activates a localized stress response that stimulated the local phosphorylation of H2AX.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the γH2AX enrichment in the vicinity of TerB sites after Tus expression was remarkably decreased upon ATRi treatment (Figure 4C–E, PP9 and PP47), implying that the Tus-TerB RFB activates a localized stress response that stimulated the local phosphorylation of H2AX.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ATRi treatment effect on γH2AX enrichment.

claim: A local activation of the intra-S checkpoint via the ATR kinase and rapid phosphorylation of H2AX could mediate the recruitment of repair factors near the damage site.
source: Together, these data suggest a local activation of the intra-S checkpoint via the ATR kinase and rapid phosphorylation of H2AX, which could mediate the recruitment of repair factors near the damage site.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ATR-dependent γH2AX enrichment data.

claim: Replication stress occurs during the S-phase of the cell cycle, when the replication machinery encounters DNA lesions that cause stalling of replicative polymerases and can be a significant cause of genomic instability.
source: Replication stress occurs during the S-phase of the cell cycle, when the replication machinery encounters DNA lesions that cause stalling of replicative polymerases and can be a significant cause of genomic instability.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: If the stalled forks cannot be processed, they can result in DNA breakage, mutations, and chromosomal rearrangements, leading to the development of many different human cancers.
source: If the stalled forks cannot be processed, they can result in DNA breakage, mutations, and chromosomal rearrangements, leading to the development of many different human cancers (Gaillard et al., 2015; Tubbs and Nussenzweig, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Tus protein efficiently binds at the TerB sequences using ChIP-qPCR and PLA in MCF7 cells.
source: We have shown that the Tus protein efficiently binds at the TerB sequences using ChIP-qPCR and PLA in MCF7 cells (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR and PLA data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The integrated system was able to cause site-specific RFB at TerB sequences when Tus was introduced with the use of the SMARD technique.
source: We confirmed that this integrated system was able to cause site-specific RFB at TerB sequences when Tus was introduced with the use of the SMARD technique and observed the accumulation of replication fork protein MCM3 upstream of TerB sequences (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by SMARD and ChIP data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The integrated Tus-TerB system acts as an efficient site-specific RFB, providing valuable insights into the local processing of a stalled single fork in human cells and its difference from global replication stress.
source: Our results indicate that the integrated Tus-TerB system acts as an efficient site-specific RFB, providing valuable insights into the local processing of a stalled single fork in human cells and its difference from global replication stress (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective data presented in the study.

claim: The site-specific replication stress leads to the accumulation of γH2AX at the site of fork block when Tus was expressed by co-immunoprecipitation of Tus and γH2AX.
source: We show that the site-specific replication stress leads to the accumulation of γH2AX at the site of fork block when Tus was expressed by co-immunoprecipitation of Tus and γH2AX (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: γH2AX is localized at the site of Tus-TerB using PLA and ChIP-qPCR assays.
source: Additionally, we confirmed that γH2AX is localized at the site of Tus-TerB using PLA and ChIP-qPCR assays (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figures 3D and 3F.

claim: The γH2AX signal is being constrained to a region of less than a kilobase from the TerB sites by torsional stress generated when the replication fork encounters the barrier.
source: We suggest that the γH2AX signal is being constrained to a region of less than a kilobase from the TerB sites by tortional stress generated when the replication fork encounters the barrier and is not influenced by well-defined topological domains that are one measure of the functional units of the genome (Dixon et al., 2012; Rao et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the localized γH2AX enrichment data and citations to prior work on topological domains.

claim: There was no observable difference in global replication profiles or the activation of global checkpoint markers such as pRPA, pCHK1, and pATR, with or without Tus protein expression.
source: Furthermore, there was no observable difference in global replication profiles or the activation of global checkpoint markers such as pRPA, pCHK1, and pATR, with or without Tus protein expression, contrasting with the differences observed in the presence and absence of HU-induced replication stress (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1a, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting, replication profile, and cell cycle data.

claim: Tus-TerB-induced replication fork stall does not activate global ATR-dependent S-phase checkpoint signaling, suggesting that a local response is occurring at the stalled replication fork.
source: We conclude that Tus-TerB-induced replication fork stall does not activate global ATR-dependent S-phase checkpoint signaling, suggesting that a local response is occurring at the stalled replication fork.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of global checkpoint activation data.

claim: Upon ATR inhibition, the enrichment of phosphorylated H2AX at TerB sites was significantly reduced when Tus was expressed, which indicates local ATR signaling is responsible for the phosphorylation of H2AX at the stalled site.
source: Interestingly, upon ATR inhibition, we observed that the enrichment of phosphorylated H2AX at TerB sites was significantly reduced when Tus was expressed, which indicates local ATR signaling is responsible for the phosphorylation of H2AX at the stalled site (Figure 4C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data with ATRi treatment shown in Figures 4C and 4E.

claim: A similar localized response had previously been observed in yeast, with a site-specific DSB in G1 cells, where there was no activation of the global checkpoint signaling, but γH2AX signaling was observed.
source: A similar localized response had previously been observed in yeast, with a site-specific DSB in G1 cells, where there was no activation of the global checkpoint signaling, but γH2AX signaling was observed (Janke et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work in yeast.

claim: This localized ATR-dependent γH2AX differs from the well-observed ATM-dependent spreading of γH2AX signal after a site-directed double-strand break.
source: This localized ATR-dependent γH2AX differs from the well-observed ATM-dependent spreading of γH2AX signal after a site-directed double-strand break (Berkovich et al., 2007; Chailleux et al., 2014; Clouaire et al., 2018; Savic et al., 2009) and suggests a distinct local intra-S phase checkpoint is being activated in response to the single RFB.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to prior work on ATM-dependent γH2AX spreading.

claim: A distinct local intra-S phase checkpoint is being activated in response to the single RFB.
source: This localized ATR-dependent γH2AX differs from the well-observed ATM-dependent spreading of γH2AX signal after a site-directed double-strand break (Berkovich et al., 2007; Chailleux et al., 2014; Clouaire et al., 2018; Savic et al., 2009) and suggests a distinct local intra-S phase checkpoint is being activated in response to the single RFB.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the localized ATR-dependent γH2AX data.

claim: In the Tus-TerB system, there is no known dissociation of the replicative helicase from the polymerase, which is responsible for the ssDNA signal.
source: In the Tus-TerB system, there is no known dissociation of the replicative helicase from the polymerase, which is responsible for the ssDNA signal.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the Tus-TerB system mechanism.

claim: ATR is expected to be activated independently of ATRIP, likely due to local changes in chromatin.
source: Therefore, just like ATM can be activated independently of the MRE11 complex (Bakkenist and Kastan, 2003), we expect that ATR is activated independently of ATRIP, likely due to local changes in chromatin that will be investigated in future studies.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on analogy to ATM activation and citation to prior work.

claim: During extensive DNA damage, the genome-wide checkpoint response activates ATR/CHK1 globally, which leads to the slowing of all replication forks in the cell, inhibition of cell cycle progression, and suppression of late origin firing.
source: During extensive DNA damage, the genome-wide checkpoint response activates ATR/CHK1 globally, which leads to the slowing of all replication forks in the cell, inhibition of cell cycle progression, and suppression of late origin firing; to provide sufficient time for DNA repair.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: A local checkpoint response occurs when one or a few replication forks encounter a DNA lesion and activates ATR/CHK1 signaling at local sites of fork stalling.
source: It has been proposed that a local checkpoint response occurs when one or a few replication forks encounter a DNA lesion and activates ATR/CHK1 signaling at local sites of fork stalling.
evidence: The claim is based on prior hypotheses in the field.

claim: The local ATR response has been hypothesized to be transient, in which the fork moves slowly only at stalled sites to promote fork stabilization, restart the stalled fork, and suppress recombination without triggering the global checkpoint response.
source: The local ATR response has been hypothesized to be transient, in which the fork moves slowly only at stalled sites to promote fork stabilization, restart the stalled fork, and suppress recombination without triggering the global checkpoint response (Iyer and Rhind, 2017; Iyer and Rhind, 2013; Kaufmann et al., 1980; Merrick et al., 2004; Saxena and Zou, 2022; Willis and Rhind, 2009; Zeman and Cimprich, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The local ATR-dependent checkpoint signaling can result in a rapid and controlled response to allow RFB resolution through the recruitment of repair factors to the damaged site.
source: We predict that the local ATR-dependent checkpoint signaling can result in a rapid and controlled response to allow RFB resolution through the recruitment of repair factors to the damaged site.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the data presented.

claim: The factors might include those involved in fork stabilization, fork reversal, fork cleavage, and homology-dependent replication restart.
source: The factors might include those involved in fork stabilization, fork reversal, fork cleavage, and homology-dependent replication restart (Saxena and Zou, 2022).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on citation to prior work.

claim: The Tus-TerB system has previously been employed in mouse embryonic stem cells to measure and investigate the DNA repair pathway choice.
source: The Tus-TerB system has previously been employed in mouse embryonic stem cells to measure and investigate the DNA repair pathway choice (Chandramouly et al., 2013; Panday et al., 2021; Willis et al., 2017; Willis et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Tus-TerB block is robust and is not dissociated by the action of DNA helicases such as PIF1.
source: The Tus-TerB block is robust and is not dissociated by the action of DNA helicases such as PIF1, corroborated in previous yeast studies that have demonstrated that the 'sweepase' RRM3 is unable to resolve this RFB (Larsen et al., 2014b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work in yeast.

claim: It is likely that the RFB is resolved either by incoming replication forks leading to termination at the TerB site or by fork cleavage.
source: Therefore, it is likely that the RFB is resolved either by incoming replication forks leading to termination at the TerB site or by fork cleavage (Larsen et al., 2014b; Willis et al., 2017; Willis et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from prior work and the robustness of the Tus-TerB block.

claim: Fork reversal at the Tus-TerB site has been observed in the yeast system, but not for the mammalian systems.
source: Fork reversal at the Tus-TerB site has been observed in the yeast system (Larsen et al., 2014b; Marie and Symington, 2022), but not for the mammalian systems, and it is unlikely that shifting the position of the RFB would make it easier to resolve.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work in yeast and inference about mammalian systems.

claim: Fork cleavage is the most likely mechanism for resolving the RFB.
source: Therefore, fork cleavage is the most likely mechanism for resolving the RFB.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the robustness of the Tus-TerB block and prior work.

claim: Previous work has shown that FANCM acts as a scaffolding protein for recruitment of different repair protein complexes involved in the stalled replication fork rescue.
source: Previous work has shown that FANCM acts as a scaffolding protein for recruitment of different repair protein complexes involved in the stalled replication fork rescue (Panday et al., 2021; Willis et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The FANCM protein is enriched at the site of the RFB induced by Tus-TerB, confirming a similar phenomenon observed in mouse cells.
source: We observed that the FANCM protein is enriched at the site of the RFB induced by Tus-TerB (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), confirming a similar phenomenon observed in mouse cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and comparison to prior work.

claim: It is yet to be determined whether FANCM recruitment to the RFB precedes local H2AX phosphorylation by ATR or whether FANCM is recruited as a consequence of the γH2AX signal to help elicit the downstream DNA damage response (DDR).
source: However, it is yet to be determined whether FANCM recruitment to the RFB precedes local H2AX phosphorylation by ATR or whether FANCM is recruited as a consequence of the γH2AX signal to help elicit the downstream DNA damage response (DDR).
evidence: The claim acknowledges uncertainty about the temporal relationship between FANCM recruitment and γH2AX phosphorylation.

claim: The protein complex, 9-1-1 (RAD9A, HUS1, RAD1), and the subsequently recruited TOPBP1, may also play a role at this local ATR-dependent intra-S checkpoint.
source: We also anticipate that the protein complex, 9-1-1 (RAD9A, HUS1, RAD1), and the subsequently recruited TOPBP1, may also play a role at this local ATR-dependent intra-S checkpoint (Helt et al., 2005; Parrilla-Castellar et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on citations to prior work.

claim: It will be important to test whether the local-S phase model remains supported when exploring endogenous lesions that occur when replication forks encounter secondary structures such as R-loops, G-quadruplexes, and common fragile sites characterized by trinucleotide repeat expansion [(CAG)n/(CTG)n].
source: While the Tus-TerB system is an important tool in deciphering signaling at individual replication forks, it will be important to test whether the local-S phase model remains supported when exploring endogenous lesions that occur when replication forks encounter secondary structures such as R-loops, G-quadruplexes, and common fragile sites characterized by trinucleotide repeat expansion [(CAG)n/(CTG)n] (Brickner et al., 2022; Bryan, 2019; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting future directions based on citations to prior work.

claim: The Tus-TerB system acts as an efficient RFB and activates local ATR checkpoint signaling at the stall site, leading to phosphorylation and accumulation of the DNA damage sensor protein γH2AX, which is dependent on the ATR kinase.
source: Overall, our results indicate that Tus-TerB system acts as an efficient RFB and activates local ATR checkpoint signaling at the stall site, leading to phosphorylation and accumulation of the DNA damage sensor protein γH2AX, which is dependent on the ATR kinase.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The local γH2AX accumulation at the stalled region would lead to the recruitment of DNA repair factors for resolution of the fork.
source: The local γH2AX accumulation at the stalled region would lead to the recruitment of DNA repair factors for resolution of the fork (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data and presented in the model in Figure 5.

claim: The site-specific fork block is dependent on the local ATR S-phase checkpoint signaling.
source: Together, our findings reveal the signaling mechanism of the Tus/TerB-induced replication block and showed that the site-specific fork block is dependent on the local ATR S-phase checkpoint signaling.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The genome contains natural impediments, which cause replication stalling such as common fragile sites, repeated sequences, non-B structures, sites of collision between transcription and replication machinery, or DNA-protein complexes.
source: The genome contains natural impediments, which cause replication stalling such as common fragile sites, repeated sequences, non-B structures, sites of collision between transcription and replication machinery, or DNA-protein complexes (Mirkin and Mirkin, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: These replication fork barriers (RFB) can impede the progression of the replication machinery and, if unresolved, lead to genomic instability, a common hallmark of aneuploidy, neurological and neuromuscular disorders, and cancer.
source: These replication fork barriers (RFB) can impede the progression of the replication machinery and, if unresolved, lead to genomic instability, a common hallmark of aneuploidy, neurological and neuromuscular disorders, and cancer.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: During replication stress, the intra-S phase checkpoint pathway can be activated at a local and global level, which is a critical step to process the DNA lesions and maintaining genome integrity.
source: During replication stress, the intra-S phase checkpoint pathway can be activated at a local and global level, which is a critical step to process the DNA lesions and maintaining genome integrity.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The S-phase checkpoint involves the uncoupling of replicative polymerases from the replicative helicase and the generation of ssDNA, which rapidly gets coated with RPA.
source: The S-phase checkpoint involves the uncoupling of replicative polymerases from the replicative helicase and the generation of ssDNA, which rapidly gets coated with RPA.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: This activates ATR/ATRIP kinase signaling with its effector kinase CHK1, plus phosphorylation of H2AX at Ser139 in response to a variety of lesions that promote cell cycle arrest, fork stabilization, and restart.
source: In turn, this activates ATR/ATRIP kinase signaling with its effector kinase CHK1, plus phosphorylation of H2AX at Ser139 in response to a variety of lesions that promote cell cycle arrest, fork stabilization, and restart (Iyer and Rhind, 2017; Iyer and Rhind, 2013; Willis and Rhind, 2009; Zeman and Cimprich, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous studies suggest that the local and global intra-S checkpoints are two distinct mechanisms that can be distinguished by the signaling intensity of detecting DNA damage.
source: Previous studies suggest that the local and global intra-S checkpoints are two distinct mechanisms that can be distinguished by the signaling intensity of detecting DNA damage (Saxena and Zou, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: It is thought that a threshold of DNA damage must be reached to activate the global checkpoint and impact cell cycle progression during replication.
source: It is thought that a threshold of DNA damage must be reached to activate the global checkpoint and impact cell cycle progression during replication (Bantele et al., 2019; Shimada et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The local checkpoint reacts to a unique replication fork stalling site, which does not impact overall cell cycle progression.
source: The local checkpoint reacts to a unique replication fork stalling site, which does not impact overall cell cycle progression.
evidence: The claim is based on prior hypotheses in the field.

claim: The proteins involved in the global replication stress response have been identified using DNA damaging agents that lead to multiple DNA lesion formation randomly throughout the genome.
source: The proteins involved in the global replication stress response have been identified using DNA damaging agents that lead to multiple DNA lesion formation randomly throughout the genome.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The mechanism and timing of the checkpoint pathway at a local scale remain largely unknown and are critical to understanding the series of processes at a single RF stall.
source: Nevertheless, the mechanism and timing of the checkpoint pathway at a local scale remain largely unknown and are critical to understanding the series of processes at a single RF stall.
evidence: The claim identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: In the Escherichia coli genome, the DNA pausing sequences called terminator (Ter) are recognized by a protein called Tus to cause a polar site-specific arrest of the RF at the end of the bacterial chromosome replication.
source: In the Escherichia coli genome, the DNA pausing sequences called terminator (Ter) are recognized by a protein called Tus to cause a polar site-specific arrest of the RF at the end of the bacterial chromosome replication (Hiasa and Marians, 1994; Hidaka et al., 1988; Mulcair et al., 2006; Roecklein et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Tus-Ter complex leads to a temporarily locked complex on DNA that can be overcome by the fork arriving in the opposite direction, displacing Tus to terminate replication.
source: The Tus-Ter complex leads to a temporarily locked complex on DNA that can be overcome by the fork arriving in the opposite direction, displacing Tus to terminate replication.
